2. Exhaustive Author & Text Analyses: John Milton (1608–1674)

John Milton stands as the titanic bridging figure between Renaissance Christian humanism and the Puritan revolution, crafting an austere, Latinate "Grand Style" that elevated English non-dramatic blank verse to its absolute zenith.
2.1 Early Lyric & Occasional Masterpieces

- **"On the Morning of Christ's Nativity" (1629)**: Composed at age 21 at Cambridge. A 27-stanza ode celebrating the Incarnation of Christ, which silences the pagan oracles and banishes the false deities of the ancient world (Apollo, Osiris, Moloch, Peor).
- **"L'Allegro" and "Il Penseroso" (c. 1631)**: Companion poems in octosyllabic couplets exploring two complementary psychological and aesthetic temperaments:
  - *"L'Allegro"* (The Cheerful Man): Welcomes Mirth (Euphrosyne), walking through the English countryside at dawn, delighting in rustic larks, courtly masques, and Shakespeare's *"wood-notes wild"*.
  - *"Il Penseroso"* (The Contemplative/Melancholy Man): Banishes vain joys, invoking divine Melancholy (*"Hail, divinest Melancholy"*), seeking solitary midnight study in a lonely tower, meditating on Plato, Hermes Trismegistus, tragic drama, and cathedral organ music.
- **"Lycidas" (1637)**: Composed for an academic memorial anthology at Cambridge commemorating the drowning of Milton's college classmate, **Edward King**, in the Irish Sea. The supreme masterpiece of the **pastoral elegy** in the English language:
  - Written in 193 lines of irregularly rhymed iambic pentameter with unrhymed lines (*canzone* structure).
  - *The Classical Pastoral Apparatus*: Invokes the Sicilian Muse (Arethusa, Mincius); mourns Lycidas as a fellow shepherd who fed flocks together; questions where the Nymphs were when their beloved died.
  - *Digression on Fame*: Milton questions the worth of dedicating one's youth to the austere craft of poetry when premature death cuts life short: *"Fame is the spur that the clear spirit doth raise / (That last infirmity of Noble mind) / To scorn delights, and live laborious dayes"*, until Phoebus Apollo intervenes, reminding the poet that true fame resides not in mortal rumors, but in the all-judging eye of Jove.
  - *Digression on Clerical Corruption (Saint Peter's Speech)*: Saint Peter ("The Pilot of the Galilean lake") carrying his two keys of gold and iron enters to deliver a ferocious attack on corrupt, worldly Anglican clergy who neglect their spiritual flocks: *"The hungry Sheep look up, and are not fed, / But swoln with wind, and the rank mist they draw, / Rot inwardly, and foul contagion spread"*, concluding with the ominous prophetic warning of retribution: *"But that two-handed engine at the door, / Stands ready to smite once, and smite no more."*
  - *Apotheosis & Resolution*: The mourning ceases as Lycidas is resurrected through the power of Christ, becoming the protective "Genius of the shore". The poem concludes with a third-person narrative shift to the youthful shepherd twitching his blue mantle and greeting the dawn: *"At last he rose, and twitch'd his Mantle blew: / To morrow to fresh Woods, and Pastures new."*
2.2 Paradise Lost (1667 in 10 Books; 1674 in 12 Books)

Composed during total blindness following the collapse of the Commonwealth, dictating lines in morning amanuensis sessions.
- **The Epic Purpose**: Stated in the opening invocation of Book I:
  > *"Of Mans First Disobedience, and the Fruit / Of that Forbidden Tree, whose mortal tast / Brought Death into the World, and all our woe, / With loss of Eden, till one greater Man / Restore us, and regain the blissful Seat, / Sing Heav'nly Muse... That to the heighth of this great Argument / I may assert Eternal Providence, / And justifie the wayes of God to men."*
- **The Verse Medium**: Milton rejected the "modern bondage of Rhyming", adopting **unrhymed iambic pentameter (English blank verse)**, enriched by epic similes, Latinate syntax (inversions, periodic sentences), and polysyllabic classical nomenclature.
- **Book-by-Book Analytical Architecture**:
  - **Book I**: Satan and the rebel angels lie stunned in the burning lake of Hell after their nine-day fall. Satan rallies his fallen host with speeches of unyielding defiance: *"What though the field be lost? / All is not lost; the unconquerable Will, / And study of revenge, immortal hate, / And courage never to submit or yield"*, declaring his famous existential manifesto: *"The mind is its own place, and in it self / Can make a Heav'n of Hell, a Hell of Heav'n... Better to reign in Hell, then serve in Heav'n."* Under the architect **Mulciber**, the fallen angels construct the towering palace of **Pandemonium**.
  - **Book II**: The Great Debate in Pandemonium over renewing war against Heaven:
    - *Moloch*: Demands immediate, reckless armed assault.
    - *Belial*: The eloquent, slothful rhetorician; counsels ignoble peace and inaction, fearing worse punishment.
    - *Mammon*: Urges peaceful exploitation of Hell's subterranean mineral wealth.
    - *Beelzebub*: Introduces Satan's covert plan to strike at God through His newly created creature, Man.
    - Satan volunteers for the perilous solo voyage across Chaos, encountering at Hell's gates his incestuous offspring: **Sin** (a woman ending in a serpent's scaly tail, ringed by barking hellhounds) and **Death** (a shadowy, crowned shape with a dart).
  - **Book III**: Opens with the luminous invocation to Holy Light: *"Hail holy Light, ofspring of Heav'n first-born"*. The celestial council: God the Father foresees Man's fall through free will (*"Sufficient to have stood, though free to fall"*); the Son of God freely offers Himself as a sacrificial ransom for mankind. Satan lands on the Sun, deceiving the archangel Uriel in the disguise of a youthful cherub.
  - **Book IV**: Satan enters the lush garden of Paradise, delivering his tortured soliloquy on Mount Niphates (*"Which way I flie is Hell; my self am Hell"*). He secretly observes Adam and Eve in blissful innocence and sexual equality (*"He for God only, she for God in him"*). Satan whispers a corrupting dream into sleeping Eve's ear at the toad's position; discovered by the guardian angels Ithuriel and Zephon.
  - **Books V–VIII**: Raphael ("the affable Archangel") visits Eden to warn Adam. Raphael recounts the **War in Heaven**: Abdiel's heroic solitary loyalty when Satan rebelled; the three-day celestial battle resolved by the Son riding in His flaming Chariot of Paternal Omnipotence; and the creation of the universe in six days. Adam discusses celestial astronomy with Raphael and recounts his own creation and marriage to Eve.
  - **Book IX: The Fall**: Satan assumes the body of the sleeping **Serpent**. Eve proposes dividing their agricultural gardening tasks; Adam reluctantly consents. Satan corners Eve alone, flattering her with extravagant rhetoric (*"Empress of this fair World, resplendent Eve"*). He argues that eating the fruit did not kill him, but gave him human speech and reason, promising that eating will elevate her to godhead (*"Ye shall be as Gods"*). Eve eats the forbidden apple:
    > *"Earth felt the wound, and Nature from her seat / Sighing through all her Works gave signs of woe, / That all was lost."*
    Eve returns to Adam; Adam, motivated by passionate human devotion rather than deception, knowingly eats the fruit to share her doom: *"he scrupled not to eat / Against his better knowledge, not deceav'd, / But fondly overcome with Femal charm."* The immediate aftermath is carnal lust followed by mutual recrimination and despair.
  - **Book X**: The Son descends to judge Adam, Eve, and the Serpent. Sin and Death construct a vast stone highway linking Hell to Earth across Chaos. Satan returns triumphantly to Pandemonium, but as he boasts of his victory, he and his legions are transformed into hissing serpents, starvingly chewing ash-filled illusory apples. Adam and Eve repent before God in genuine sorrow.
  - **Books XI–XII**: The archangel Michael descends to expel the fallen couple from Paradise. Michael reveals a prophetic vision of human history from Cain and Abel, through the Flood, the Tower of Babel, Abraham, and the Incarnation of Christ to the Day of Judgment. Adam attains the spiritual wisdom of the **"paradise within thee, happier farr"**. The epic concludes with Adam and Eve hand-in-hand stepping into the fallen world:
    > *"Some natural tears they drop'd, but wip'd them soon; / The World was all before them, where to choose / Thir place of rest, and Providence thir guide: / They hand in hand with wandring steps and slow, / Through Eden took thir solitarie way."*
2.3 Samson Agonistes (1671)

Milton's monumental closet drama modeled strictly on ancient Greek tragedy (Sophocles, Euripides), observing the classical unities of time (single day), place (prison at Gaza), and action:
- **Biographical Parallel**: Depicts the blind, captive biblical Hebrew judge **Samson** grinding grain at the Philistine mill, reflecting Milton's own blindness, political defeat, and isolation after the Restoration.
- **The Agonists**: Samson is visited by successive temptors:
  - *Manoa*: His elderly father, offering to ransom him for a quiet, ignoble retirement.
  - *Dalila*: His traitorous Philistine wife, pleading conjugal weakness, whom Samson fiercely denounces as a "hyena".
  - *Harapha*: The bragging Philistine giant, whom Samson dares to single combat.
- **The Catastrophe**: Samson is summoned to perform feats of physical strength at the feast of the pagan god Dagon. Feeling "rousing motions" within his soul, Samson grasps the two central pillars of the temple, pulling the roof down upon himself and the Philistine nobility. The Chorus concludes with the famous Aristotelian cathartic lines: *"His servants he with new acquist / Of true experience from this great event / With peace and consolation hath dismist, / And calm of mind, all passion spent."*
3. Exhaustive Author & Text Analyses: John Dryden (1631–1700)

John Dryden dominated the Restoration literary landscape with such supreme authority that the period is routinely designated the **"Age of Dryden"**. Appointed England's first official **Poet Laureate** (1668) and Historiographer Royal (1670).
3.1 Absalom and Achitophel (1681)

The finest political verse satire in the English language, composed in heroic couplets to defend King Charles II during the **Exclusion Crisis** (1679–1681):
- **The Biblical Allegory**: Dryden mapped contemporary English politics onto the biblical rebellion of King David's son Absalom (2 Samuel):
  - **King David** = **King Charles II** (benevolent, amorous, father of many illegitimate offspring).
  - **Absalom** = **James Scott, Duke of Monmouth** (Charles II's handsome, illegitimate, Protestant son).
  - **Achitophel** = **Anthony Ashley Cooper, 1st Earl of Shaftesbury** (Whig leader scheming to exclude the Catholic Duke of York from the throne).
  - **Zimri** = **George Villiers, 2nd Duke of Buckingham** (satirized for erratic dilettantism).
- **The Portrait of Achitophel (Shaftesbury)**: Masterpiece of forensic character assassination:
  > *"Of these the false Achitophel was first: / A Name to all succeeding Ages Curst. / For close Designs, and crooked Counsels fit; / Sagacious, Bold, and Turbulent of wit: / Restless, unfixt in Principles and Place; / In Pow'r unpleas'd, impatient of Disgrace. / A fiery Soul, which working out its way, / Fretted the Pigmy Body to decay: / And o'r-inform'd the Tenement of Clay. / A Daring Pilot in extremity; / Pleas'd with the Danger, when the Waves went high / He sought the Storms; but for a Calm unfit, / Would Steer too nigh the Sands, to boast his Wit."*
- **The Portrait of Zimri (Buckingham)**:
  > *"A man so various, that he seem'd to be / Not one, but all Mankinds Epitome. / Stiff in Opinions, always in the wrong; / Was everything by starts, and nothing long: / But, in the course of one revolving Moon, / Was Chymist, Fidler, States-Man, and Buffoon."*
3.2 Mac Flecknoe (1682)

The pioneering masterpiece that established the English **Mock-Heroic** genre, written to ridicule Dryden's literary rival, the Whig playwright **Thomas Shadwell**:
- **Premise**: **Richard Flecknoe** (an actual, notoriously poor Irish poet who had recently died) reigns as the supreme absolute monarch over the global kingdom of Non-sense. Feeling age creep upon him, Flecknoe resolves to choose an heir who resembles him in absolute, uncorrupted stupidity:
  > *"All humane things are subject to decay, / And, when Fate summons, Monarchs must obey: / This Flecknoe found, who, like Augustus, young / Was call'd to Empire, and had govern'd long: / In Prose and Verse, was own'd, without dispute / Through all the Realms of Non-sense, absolute... / Shadwell alone my perfect image bears, / Mature in dullness from his tender years. / Shadwell alone, of all my Sons, is he / Who stands confirm'd in full stupidity. / The rest to some faint meaning make pretence, / But Shadwell never deviates into sense."*
- **The Coronation**: Flecknoe crowns Shadwell as the new King of Dullness in a decrepit brothel district of London, seated on a throne of toilet paper and unread books, while poppies are scattered upon his temples. The poem concludes with Flecknoe falling through a trapdoor, leaving his double-mantle of stupidity to drop upon Shadwell (a parody of Elijah's mantle descending upon Elisha).
3.3 Religious Confessions

- **Religio Laici (1682)**: ("A Layman's Faith"): A rational defense of the Anglican Church against both Catholic papal infallibility and radical Puritan deism, composed in sober, argumentative heroic couplets.
- **The Hind and the Panther (1687)**: Following his conversion to Roman Catholicism under the reign of James II, Dryden composed this extraordinary 2,500-line allegorical beast fable:
  - **The Milk-White Hind**: Represents the Roman Catholic Church (*"A Milk white Hind, immortal and unchang'd, / Fed on the lawn, and in the forrest rang'd; / Without unspotted, innocent within, / She fear'd no danger, for she knew no sin"*).
  - **The Panther**: Represents the Church of England (noble, beautiful, but spotted with theological compromise).
  - Other beasts represent nonconformist sects: The **Wolf** (Presbyterians), The **Fox** (Socinians), The **Bear** (Independents), and The **Boar** (Anabaptists).
4. Exhaustive Author & Text Analyses: Alexander Pope (1688–1744)

The supreme master of Augustan verse, the closed heroic couplet, and intellectual satire. Due to his Roman Catholicism and childhood tuberculosis of the spine (Pott's disease), Pope was barred from university, public office, and physical vigor (standing barely 4 feet 6 inches tall), pouring his formidable intellectual energy into his poetry.
4.1 An Essay on Criticism (1711)

Composed when Pope was barely 23 years old; a brilliant synthesis of classical Horatian poetics (*Ars Poetica*) and Boileau's *L'Art poétique*, establishing the critical laws of Augustan taste:
- **Famous Axioms**:
  - *"A little Learning is a dang'rous Thing; / Drink deep, or taste not the Pierian Spring."*
  - *"To Err is Humane; to Forgive, Divine."*
  - *"True Wit is Nature to Advantage drest, / What oft was Thought, but ne'er so well Exprest."*
  - *"Fools rush in where Angels fear to tread."*
- **The Principle of Sound and Sense**: Pope argues that poetic meter must organically reflect the physical action described:
  > *"True Ease in Writing comes from Art, not Chance, / As those move easiest who have learn'd to dance. / 'Tis not enough no Harshness gives Offence, / The Sound must seem an Eccho to the Sense. / Soft is the Strain when Zephyr gently blows, / And the smooth Stream in smoother Numbers flows; / But when loud Surges lash the sounding Shore, / The hoarse, rough Verse shou'd like the Torrent roar. / When Ajax strives, some Rock's vast Weight to throw, / The Line too labours, and the Words move slow; / Not so, when swift Camilla scours the Plain, / Flies o'er the unbending Corn, and skims along the Main."*
4.2 The Rape of the Lock (1712 in 2 Cantos; 1714 in 5 Cantos)

The greatest **Mock-Heroic (Heroi-Comical)** poem in world literature:
- **Historical Occasion**: Composed at the request of Pope's friend **John Caryll** to reconcile two prominent Catholic families after Lord Petre playfully snipped a lock of hair from the head of the society belle **Arabella Fermor**:
  > *"What dire Offence from am'rous Causes springs, / What mighty Contests rise from trivial Things, / I sing—This Verse to Caryll, Muse! is due."*
- **The Heroic Parody**: Parodies the monumental apparatus of Homer's *Iliad* and Milton's *Paradise Lost* to narrate a petty aristocratic flirtation:
  - *The Epic Invocation & Dream*: Belinda is warned in a morning dream by her guardian sylph **Ariel**.
  - *The Arming of the Hero (Belinda's Toilet, Canto I)*: Belinda prepares at her dressing table; cosmetic makeup, combs, and pins are described as sacred armor, and her reflection is worshipped as a goddess: *"Now awful Beauty puts on all its Arms; / The Fair each moment rises in her Charms... Puffs, Powders, Patches, Bibles, Billet-doux."*
  - *The Rosicrucian Machinery (1714 Edition)*: Pope added supernatural elemental spirits adapted from the French Rosicrucian treatise *Le Comte de Gabalis*:
    - **Sylphs** (Air): Protect chaste virgins (headed by Ariel).
    - **Nymphs** (Water): Soft, yielding women.
    - **Gnomes** (Earth): Prudes and gossips (headed by Umbriel).
    - **Salamanders** (Fire): Scolds and angry women.
  - *The Epic Journey & The Battle of Ombre (Cantos II–III)*: Belinda sails up the Thames to Hampton Court Palace (*"Where Thou, Great Anna! whom three Realms obey, / Dost sometimes Counsel take—and sometimes Tea"*). The card game of **Ombre** is described as a ferocious epic military cavalry charge between Kings, Queens, and Knaves.
  - *The Severing of the Lock (Canto III)*: The Baron, armed with a pair of scissors (*"the fatal Engine"*), snips the prized lock of hair while Belinda sips coffee, cleanly bisecting an unfortunate sylph who intervenes (who instantly rejoins, echoing Milton's wounded spirits).
  - *The Underworld Descent (The Cave of Spleen, Canto IV)*: The melancholy gnome Umbriel descends to the subterranean Cave of Spleen to fetch a bag of sighs, sobs, and tears from the goddess Spleen, releasing them over Belinda.
  - *Clarissa's Speech on Good Humour (Canto V, added in 1717)*: Pope's moral center, urging women to value enduring good sense and virtue over transient physical beauty: *"Beauties in vain their pretty Eyes may roll; / Charms strike the Sight, but Merit wins the Soul."*
  - *The Final Melee & Apotheosis*: A comic battle with bodkins, snuff, and frowns. The lock of hair vanishes in the scuffle, ascending into the heavens as a **new constellation (a comet)** to immortalize Belinda's name forever.
4.3 The Dunciad (1728; Final 4-Book Edition, 1743)

Pope's apocalyptic mock-epic masterpiece of literary satire, dedicated to Jonathan Swift:
- **Plot**: The goddess **Dulness** seeks a new monarch to rule her vast empire of bad writing, pedantry, and commercial hacks (Grub Street).
- **The Heroes**: In the early versions (1728), the Shakespearean editor **Lewis Theobald** (who had exposed errors in Pope's edition of Shakespeare) was crowned King of the Dunces; in the final 1743 edition, Pope substituted the Whig Poet Laureate and actor-dramatist **Colley Cibber** as the supreme Dunce.
- **The Cosmic Catastrophe (Book IV)**: Dulness yawns, unleashing an apocalyptic wave of chaos, pedantry, and intellectual darkness over Britain. The poem ends with one of the most sublime passages in English poetry:
  > *"She comes! she comes! the gloomy Sovereign quakes, / And at her Footstool Chaos drops and shakes... / Thy hand, great Anarch! lets the curtain fall, / And Universal Darkness buries All."*
4.4 An Essay on Man (1733–1734)

Four philosophical epistles in heroic couplets addressed to Henry St. John, Lord Bolingbroke, vindicating the divine order of the cosmos:
- **Core Philosophy**: A poetic synthesis of Christian deism and Leibnizian optimism (*"Whatever is, is right"*):
  - Man occupies an essential, intermediate position on the **Great Chain of Being** between animals and angels:
  > *"Know then thyself, presume not God to scan; / The proper study of Mankind is Man. / Plac'd on this isthmus of a middle state, / A Being darkly wise, and rudely great: / With too much knowledge for the Sceptic side, / With too much weakness for the Stoic's pride, / He hangs between; in doubt to act, or rest; / In doubt to deem himself a God, or Beast."*
5. Exhaustive Author & Text Analyses: Dr. Samuel Johnson (1709–1784)

The supreme critical moralist, lexicographer, and arbiter of eighteenth-century literary prose and verse. Johnson practiced verse satire in the moral, somber tradition of the Roman satirist **Juvenal**.
5.1 London (1738) and The Vanity of Human Wishes (1749)

- **London (1738)**: An imitation of **Juvenal's Third Satire**. The impoverished, honest poet Thales abandons the corrupt, crime-ridden metropolis of London to find rural retirement in Wales. Satirizes the commercial corruption of Sir Robert Walpole's Whig ministry:
  > *"This mournful truth is ev'ry where confess'd, / SLOW RISES WORTH, BY POVERTY DEPRESS'D."*
- **The Vanity of Human Wishes (1749)**: An imitation of **Juvenal's Tenth Satire**; Johnson's poetic masterpiece in heavy, majestic, philosophically profound heroic couplets:
  - Explores the universal tragedy of human ambition across history: statesmen, scholars, military conquerors, and beauties all seek wealth, power, and long life, only to find misery and ruin.
  - *The Fall of Cardinal Wolsey*: Reaches zenith of worldly power only to fall into instant royal disgrace and ruin: *"At length his sov'reign frowns—the train of state / Mark the keen glance, and watch the sign to hate."*
  - *The Scholar's Tragedy*: The aspiring intellectual faces poverty, neglect, and patronizing insult:
    > *"There mark what ills the scholar's life assail, / Toil, envy, want, the patron, and the jail."*
  - *Charles XII of Sweden*: The mighty warrior-king who terrified Europe is defeated at Poltava and dies by an ignominious stray bullet at an obscure siege:
    > *"He left the Name, at which the World grew pale, / To point a Moral, or adorn a Tale."*
  - *The Christian Stoic Resolution*: The poem rejects nihilistic cynicism, concluding that peace is achieved through faith, patience, love, and resignation to God's eternal will.
6. Technical Conventions, Forms & Metrics
6.1 The Closed Heroic Couplet: Anatomical Breakdown

The primary verse instrument of the Restoration and Augustan eras:
- **Metrical Rigor**: Strictly ten syllables (iambic pentameter).
- **Syntactic Closure**: The sentence or complete thought concludes strictly at the end of the second rhymed line (end-stopped), avoiding enjambment.
- **The Internal Caesura & Chiasmus**: A rhythmic pause dividing each line into balanced grammatical halves.
- **Antithesis**: Sharp rhetorical contrast of opposing concepts balanced symmetrically across the caesura:
  - *"Favours to none, || to all she Smiles extends"*
  - *"Oft she rejects, || but never once offends"*
  - *"Charms strike the Sight, || but Merit wins the Soul"*
6.2 The Mock-Heroic Epic (Heroi-Comical) Formula

A satirical genre that burlesques classical epic conventions by treating a trivial, frivolous modern subject with the high grand style and supernatural machinery of Homer, Virgil, and Milton:
1. **Epic Invocation & Dedication**: Stating a monumental theme born of trivial origins (*"What dire Offence from am'rous Causes springs..."*).
2. **Supernatural Machinery**: Substituting divine gods and angels with miniature, whimsical sprites (Sylphs, Gnomes in Pope; Flecknoe's coronation in Dryden).
3. **The Arming of the Hero**: Parodying the arming of Achilles or Aeneas through domestic dressing, cosmetics, and wigs.
4. **The Epic Game / Tournament**: Parodying funeral games and warfare through card games (Ombre in Pope) or urination/swimming contests (the sewer games of *The Dunciad*).
5. **The Descent to the Underworld (Nekuia)**: Visiting subterranean allegorical realms (The Cave of Spleen).
6. **The Climactic Combat & Apotheosis**: Ending with physical brawls utilizing domestic weapons (snuff, bodkins) and immortalizing the object among the stars.
7. Comparative Analysis Matrices
7.1 Miltonic Grand Blank Verse vs. Augustan Heroic Couplets

| Dimension | John Milton (*Paradise Lost*) | John Dryden & Alexander Pope |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Meter & Rhyme** | Unrhymed Iambic Pentameter (Blank Verse) | Closed Heroic Couplets (*aa bb cc*) |
| **Syntax** | Highly Latinate, extensive inversions, long periodic sentences spanning dozens of lines | Crisp, balanced, antithetical, strictly end-stopped couplets |
| **Enjambment** | Continuous, flowing run-on lines (*verse paragraphs*) | Rigorously suppressed; thoughts contained within two lines |
| **Aesthetic Register** | The Sublime, Biblical grandeur, Cosmic expanse | Wit (*ingenium*), Urban irony, Polished social decorum |
| **Primary Theme** | Fall of Man, Free Will, Divine Providence | Social folly, Literary dullness, Political factionalism |
7.2 The Great Satires: *Absalom and Achitophel* vs. *The Rape of the Lock* vs. *The Dunciad*

| Text | Author | Satirical Mode | Target / Occasion | Resolution |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Absalom and Achitophel** | John Dryden | Political Biblical Allegory | Earl of Shaftesbury & Whig Exclusion Crisis | King David (Charles II) speaks; royal authority reasserted. |
| **The Rape of the Lock** | Alexander Pope | Heroi-Comical / Mock-Heroic | Petty feud between Petre & Fermor families | The lock ascends to heaven as an immortal constellation. |
| **The Dunciad** | Alexander Pope | Apocalyptic Mock-Epic | Bad writers, commercial print culture, Cibber | Universal Darkness buries science, art, and civilization. |
| **The Vanity of Human Wishes** | Samuel Johnson | Juvenalian Moral / Stoic Satire | Universal futility of human worldly desires | Christian faith, patience, and resignation to God. |

| **1738** | Samuel Johnson, *London* | Juvenalian imitation attacking Walpole's London. |
| **1743** | Pope, *The Dunciad in Four Books* | Apocalyptic final version crowning Colley Cibber. |
| **1744** | Death of Alexander Pope | Formal close of the High Augustan poetic era. |
| **1749** | Samuel Johnson, *The Vanity of Human Wishes* | Pinnacle of 18th-century philosophical and moral verse. |
9. 50 High-Yield Exam One-Liners & Trap Alerts

1. **Milton's Verse Rejection**: In the preface to the 1668 reissue of *Paradise Lost*, Milton proudly defended blank verse, calling rhyme *"the Invention of a barbarous Age, to set off wretched matter and lame Meeter."*
2. **The 10 to 12 Books Split**: *Paradise Lost* was originally published in 1667 in **10 books**; in the 1674 second edition, Milton divided Books VII and X into two each (creating Books VII, VIII, XI, XII) to form **12 books** mirroring Virgil's *Aeneid*.
3. **Milton's Epic Stated Purpose**: *"That to the heighth of this great Argument / I may assert Eternal Providence, / And justifie the wayes of God to men"* (Book I).
4. **Satan's Existential Motto**: *"The mind is its own place, and in it self / Can make a Heav'n of Hell, a Hell of Heav'n"* (Book I).
5. **Pandemonium's Architect**: The palace of Hell, Pandemonium, was designed by **Mulciber** (the classical Vulcan/Hephaestus).
6. **The Four Speakers in Pandemonium**: Moloch (open war), Belial (ignoble peace/sloth), Mammon (peaceful mining/wealth), Beelzebub (seducing God's new creature, Man).
7. **Sin and Death's Origin**: Sin sprang fully formed from Satan's head in Heaven (parodying Athena from Zeus); Satan incestuously impregnated Sin, who gave birth to Death.
8. **The Blindness Invocation**: Book III of *Paradise Lost* opens with Milton's luminous hymn to Holy Light (*"Hail holy Light, ofspring of Heav'n first-born"*), lamenting his loss of sight.
9. **Blake on Milton**: William Blake famously wrote in *The Marriage of Heaven and Hell* (1790): *"The reason Milton wrote in fetters when he wrote of Angels & God, and at liberty when of Devils & Hell, is because he was a true Poet and of the Devils party without knowing it."*
10. **The Unfallen Hair**: In Book IV, Eve's hair is described as flowing in unadorned golden tresses, expressing natural innocence: *"in wanton ringlets wav'd / As the Vine curls her tendrils."*
11. **The Serpent's Instrument**: In Book IX, Satan chooses the **Serpent** as his disguise because it was *"subtlest Beast of all the Field"*.
12. **Eve's Sin Motivation**: Eve falls because of intellectual ambition and pride, believing Satan's flattery that eating the fruit will transform her into a goddess (*"Ye shall be as Gods"*).
13. **Adam's Sin Motivation**: Adam is not deceived by Satan's arguments, but eats the fruit out of passionate human attachment to Eve, choosing to die with her rather than live without her.
14. **Nature's Groan**: When Eve eats the fruit, *"Earth felt the wound, and Nature from her seat / Sighing through all her Works gave signs of woe, / That all was lost."*
15. **The Transformation into Serpents**: In Book X, when Satan returns to Pandemonium to boast of his conquest, God transforms him and all the fallen angels into hissing serpents chewing bitter ash.
16. **The Final Lines of Paradise Lost**: Adam and Eve leave Eden hand in hand: *"The World was all before them, where to choose / Thir place of rest, and Providence thir guide"*.
17. **Lycidas Occasion**: Composed in 1637 for **Edward King**, a Cambridge classmate who drowned when his ship sank off the coast of Wales.
18. **The Two Keys in Lycidas**: Saint Peter carries two keys: the golden key opens the gates of Heaven, while the iron key shuts them fast.
19. **The "Two-Handed Engine"**: An enigmatic crux in *Lycidas* (*"that two-handed engine at the door"*), critically interpreted as Parliament, the two houses of Parliament, the executioner's two-handed axe, or the Old and New Testaments.
20. **L'Allegro and Il Penseroso Meters**: Composed in light, musical octosyllabic couplets (iambic tetrameter).
21. **Samson Agonistes Meaning**: "Agonistes" is Greek for "the wrestler", "the athlete", or "the combatant in public games".
22. **The Tragic Unities in Samson**: Milton strictly observed Aristotle's three unities of time (one day), place (Gaza prison), and action.
23. **First Official Poet Laureate**: John Dryden was appointed England's first official Poet Laureate by King Charles II in **1668**.
24. **The Exclusion Crisis**: The historical backdrop of *Absalom and Achitophel*, where Shaftesbury's Whigs sought to exclude James, Duke of York, due to his Roman Catholicism.
25. **David's Polygamy in Absalom**: Dryden wittily defends Charles II's promiscuity in the opening lines: *"In pious times, ere Priest-craft did begin, / Before Polygamy was made a sin"*.
26. **Zimri's Identity**: The erratic character Zimri in *Absalom and Achitophel* represents **George Villiers, 2nd Duke of Buckingham**.
27. **Mac Flecknoe Subtitle**: The complete subtitle is: *Mac Flecknoe: or, A satyr upon the True-Blew-Protestant Poet, T.S.*
28. **Dryden's Target in Mac Flecknoe**: Playwright **Thomas Shadwell**, ridiculed as the undisputed heir to the kingdom of Absolute Dullness.
29. **"Never Deviates into Sense"**: Dryden's devastating verdict on Shadwell: *"The rest to some faint meaning make pretence, / But Shadwell never deviates into sense."*
30. **The Beasts in The Hind and the Panther**: The Milk-White Hind is the Roman Catholic Church; the Panther is the Church of England; the Wolf is the Presbyterians.
31. **Pope's Childhood Illness**: Alexander Pope suffered from Pott's disease (tubercular curvature of the spine), resulting in stunted growth and chronic physical pain (*"this long disease, my life"*).
32. **The Pierian Spring**: *"A little Learning is a dang'rous Thing; / Drink deep, or taste not the Pierian Spring"* appears in Pope's *An Essay on Criticism*.
33. **True Wit Definition**: *"True Wit is Nature to Advantage drest, / What oft was Thought, but ne'er so well Exprest"* appears in *An Essay on Criticism*.
34. **Rape of the Lock Historical Figures**: Arabella Fermor is **Belinda**; Lord Petre is **the Baron**; John Caryll commissioned the poem.
35. **The Four Rosicrucian Elementals**: Sylphs (Air/Chaste virgins), Gnomes (Earth/Prudes), Nymphs (Water/Yielding), Salamanders (Fire/Scolds).
36. **Belinda's Guardian Sylph**: **Ariel** is the chief sylph who warns Belinda in her morning dream.
37. **The Cave of Spleen**: In Canto IV, the gnome **Umbriel** journeys to the Cave of Spleen to obtain a bag filled with sighs, screams, and tears.
38. **The Game of Ombre**: Canto III describes the popular three-handed Spanish card game of **Ombre** as a miniature military war between Kings and Queens.
39. **Clarissa's Moral**: Added to Canto V in 1717 to highlight the poem's serious moral: physical charms fade, but good sense and moral virtue endure (*"Charms strike the Sight, but Merit wins the Soul"*).
40. **Fate of the Lock**: The cut lock ascends into the sky and transforms into a shining **comet** (constellation).
41. **The Hero of The Dunciad**: Originally Lewis Theobald (1728); replaced in 1743 by the actor and Poet Laureate **Colley Cibber**.
42. **The Final Line of The Dunciad**: *"And Universal Darkness buries All"*—signifying the collapse of civilization under the yawning goddess Dulness.
43. **Pope's Great Chain of Being**: In *An Essay on Man*, Pope asserts that man occupies a middle link between beasts and angels, concluding: *"Whatever is, is right."*
44. **"The Proper Study of Mankind"**: *"Know then thyself, presume not God to scan; / The proper study of Mankind is Man"* opens Epistle II of *An Essay on Man*.
45. **Scriblerus Club Members**: Alexander Pope, Jonathan Swift, John Gay, Thomas Parnell, and Dr. John Arbuthnot.
46. **Dr. Johnson's London Model**: Samuel Johnson's *London* (1738) is a direct neoclassical imitation of **Juvenal's Third Satire**.
47. **Slow Rises Worth**: *"SLOW RISES WORTH, BY POVERTY DEPRESS'D"* was printed in capital letters by Johnson in *London*.
48. **The Vanity of Human Wishes Model**: A direct imitation of **Juvenal's Tenth Satire**.
49. **Charles XII of Sweden**: In *The Vanity of Human Wishes*, Charles XII's life exemplifies the futility of military conquest: *"He left the Name, at which the World grew pale, / To point a Moral, or adorn a Tale."*
50. **The Scholar's Miseries**: In *The Vanity of Human Wishes*, Johnson lists the five trials of an intellectual: *"Toil, envy, want, the patron, and the jail"* (originally *garret*, changed to *patron* after Lord Chesterfield's slight).

mcqs.question: In Book I of *Paradise Lost*, which fallen angel is celebrated as the grand architect who designed the palace of Pandemonium?
mcqs.explanation: Mulciber (the Roman god Vulcan/Hephaestus) is described in Book I as the divine architect who built towers in Heaven and subsequently erected Pandemonium, the golden high capital of Satan and his peers in Hell.

mcqs.question: What was the central reason stated by John Milton for rejecting rhyme in his 1668 prefatory note to *Paradise Lost*?
options: Rhyme was too difficult for long narrative works
Rhyme was the invention of a barbarous age and constituted modern bondage
The English language lacked sufficient monosyllabic rhyming words
Ancient Greek and Roman epics were exclusively composed in French couplets
mcqs.explanation: In his note on "The Verse", Milton famously denounced rhyme as *"the Invention of a barbarous Age, to set off wretched matter and lame Meeter"*, celebrating blank verse as restoring English poetry to ancient epic liberty.

mcqs.question: In Milton's *Lycidas*, who delivers the devastating speech condemning the corrupt clergy as hireling shepherds who let their sheep "rot inwardly"?
options: The Pilot of the Galilean Lake (Saint Peter)
mcqs.explanation: Saint Peter ("The Pilot of the Galilean lake"), carrying the keys of gold and iron, interrupts the pastoral lament to denounce corrupt Anglican priests who climb into the fold for worldly wealth, warning of the "two-handed engine at the door".

mcqs.question: In John Dryden's political allegory *Absalom and Achitophel*, which contemporary English politician is satirized under the guise of Achitophel?
options: Anthony Ashley Cooper, 1st Earl of Shaftesbury
mcqs.explanation: Achitophel represents Anthony Ashley Cooper, 1st Earl of Shaftesbury, the ambitious Whig politician who plotted to exclude the Catholic Duke of York by elevating Charles II's illegitimate son, Monmouth (Absalom).

mcqs.question: Who is crowned as the monarch of the global realm of Non-sense in John Dryden's mock-heroic satire *Mac Flecknoe*?
mcqs.explanation: In *Mac Flecknoe*, the aging king Richard Flecknoe chooses the Whig playwright Thomas Shadwell as his true literary heir because Shadwell "alone stands confirm'd in full stupidity" and "never deviates into sense".

mcqs.question: What supernatural Rosicrucian spirits protect chaste maidens in the 1714 five-canto edition of Alexander Pope's *The Rape of the Lock*?
mcqs.explanation: In Pope's adaptation of Rosicrucian lore, Sylphs are aerial spirits who protect the purity and honor of young virgin maidens, commanded by Ariel.

mcqs.question: Which character in *The Rape of the Lock* delivers the speech on "good humour" in Canto V, emphasizing that "Charms strike the Sight, but Merit wins the Soul"?
mcqs.explanation: Clarissa's speech was inserted by Pope in the 1717 edition to articulate the moral center of the poem, arguing that since physical beauty inevitably fades, women must cultivate good sense and virtue.

mcqs.question: In Alexander Pope's *The Dunciad* (1743 final edition), who was crowned by the goddess Dulness as the supreme King of the Dunces?
mcqs.explanation: While Lewis Theobald was the hero of the original 1728 edition, Pope replaced him in the 1743 four-book version with Colley Cibber, the Whig Poet Laureate and theatrical manager.

mcqs.question: The famous critical axiom *"True Wit is Nature to Advantage drest, / What oft was Thought, but ne'er so well Exprest"* appears in which work?
options: John Dryden's *An Essay of Dramatic Poesy*
mcqs.explanation: In *An Essay on Criticism* (1711), Pope defines neoclassical wit not as bizarre novelty, but as the polished, memorable expression of universal natural truth.

mcqs.question: Samuel Johnson's poem *The Vanity of Human Wishes* (1749) is a formal neoclassical imitation of which classical Roman satire?
mcqs.explanation: *The Vanity of Human Wishes* is an imitation of Juvenal's Tenth Satire (which examines the universal folly of worldly prayers), whereas Johnson's earlier poem *London* (1738) is an imitation of Juvenal's Third Satire.

mcqs.question: In Book IX of *Paradise Lost*, what primary psychological emotion compels Adam to eat the forbidden fruit after Eve has fallen?
options: Intellectual curiosity to gain secret knowledge
Passionate human love and unwillingness to be separated from Eve
Defiant hatred and anger toward God's law
mcqs.explanation: Milton explicitly emphasizes that Adam was "not deceav'd, / But fondly overcome with Femal charm", consciously choosing mortal death alongside Eve rather than eternal life without her.

mcqs.question:
Match the allegorical beast in John Dryden's *The Hind and the Panther* (List I) with the religious denomination it represents (List II):
| List I (Beast) | List II (Denomination) |
| :--- | :--- |
| a. The Milk-White Hind | 1. The Roman Catholic Church |
| b. The Panther | 2. The Church of England |
| c. The Wolf | 3. The Presbyterians |
| d. The Fox | 4. The Socinians |
**Options:**
mcqs.explanation: The Hind represents Roman Catholicism; the Panther represents Anglicanism; the Wolf represents Presbyterianism; and the Fox represents Socinianism.

mcqs.question: In Milton's closet drama *Samson Agonistes*, who visits the blind captive Samson offering to pay a ransom to secure his release?
mcqs.explanation: Manoa, Samson's aged father, attempts to negotiate a monetary ransom with the Philistine lords, but Samson refuses an ignoble, inactive retirement.

mcqs.question: In *The Rape of the Lock*, what is the name of the gnome who journeys to the subterranean Cave of Spleen to procure a bag of sighs and tears?
mcqs.explanation: Umbriel is the dusky, melancholy gnome who descends into the Cave of Spleen in Canto IV to bring back a vial of sorrow and a bag of shrieks to pour over Belinda.

mcqs.question: Which card game is described as a monumental epic battle of kings, queens, and soldiers in Canto III of *The Rape of the Lock*?
mcqs.explanation: The three-handed card game of Ombre (from the Spanish *hombre*) is depicted as a miniature military conflict where Belinda defeats the Baron.

mcqs.question: Which famous couplet from Samuel Johnson's *The Vanity of Human Wishes* summarizes the tragic military career of Charles XII of Sweden?
options: *"He left the Name, at which the World grew pale, / To point a Moral, or adorn a Tale."*
*"There mark what ills the scholar's life assail, / Toil, envy, want, the patron, and the jail."*
*"Must helpless man, in ignorance sedate, / Roll darkling down the torrent of his fate?"*
mcqs.explanation: Charles XII's sudden, inglorious death at the siege of Fredrikshald is immortalized in this celebrated couplet.

mcqs.question: In Milton's *Paradise Lost*, which archangel leads Adam up a high hill in Books XI and XII to reveal the future history of mankind?
mcqs.explanation: The archangel Michael is dispatched to expel the fallen pair from Eden and displays the prophetic panorama of human biblical history to Adam.

mcqs.question: Who was the real-life historical model for the character of Zimri in John Dryden's *Absalom and Achitophel*?
options: Sir George Savile, Marquess of Halifax
mcqs.explanation: Dryden satirized the eccentric, fickle Duke of Buckingham as Zimri ("Was everything by starts, and nothing long"), partially in retaliation for Buckingham mocking Dryden as Bayes in *The Rehearsal* (1671).

mcqs.question:
Arrange the following poetic works in chronological order of their initial publication:
1. Alexander Pope, *The Rape of the Lock* (5-Canto Edition)  
2. John Milton, *Paradise Lost* (10-Book First Edition)  
3. John Dryden, *Absalom and Achitophel*  
4. Samuel Johnson, *The Vanity of Human Wishes*  
**Options:**
mcqs.explanation: *Paradise Lost* appeared in 1667; *Absalom and Achitophel* in 1681; the 5-canto *Rape of the Lock* in 1714; and *The Vanity of Human Wishes* in 1749.

mcqs.question:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R):
**Assertion (A):** In *The Dunciad*, Alexander Pope depicts the triumph of the goddess Dulness not as lighthearted comedic fun, but as a catastrophic cultural apocalypse.  
**Reason (R):** Pope believed that the commercialization of printing and the rise of unprincipled hack writers on Grub Street threatened to subvert classical learning, rationality, and political integrity.  
**Options:**
options:
and the other as Reason (R):
**Assertion (A):** In *The Dunciad*, Alexander Pope depicts the triumph of the goddess Dulness not as lighthearted comedic fun, but as a catastrophic cultural apocalypse.  
**Reason (R):** Pope believed that the commercialization of printing and the rise of unprincipled hack writers on Grub Street threatened to subvert classical learning, rationality, and political integrity.  
**Options:**  
(A) Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
mcqs.explanation: Pope viewed the proliferation of commercial scribblers as an existential threat to classical humanist civilization, culminating in the terrifying final vision where "Universal Darkness buries All".

mcqs.question: Which satirical poem by Samuel Johnson contains the line: *"There mark what ills the scholar's life assail, / Toil, envy, want, the patron, and the jail"*?
options: *On the Death of Dr. Robert Levet*
mcqs.explanation: This line occurs in *The Vanity of Human Wishes*; Johnson famously altered "the garret" to "the patron" following his bitter disappointment with Lord Chesterfield over his *Dictionary*.

mcqs.question: In Book IV of *Paradise Lost*, what does Satan whisper into Eve's ear while she sleeps in the bower, disguised in which creature's form?
mcqs.explanation: The guardian angels Ithuriel and Zephon discover Satan squatting like a toad at the ear of Eve, attempting to poison her thoughts with vanity and discontent.

mcqs.question: Alexander Pope's philosophical dictum *"Whatever is, is right"* serves as the culminating moral statement of which poem?
mcqs.explanation: In Epistle I of *An Essay on Man*, Pope asserts that from God's cosmic perspective, apparent human discord is harmony not understood, concluding: *"Whatever is, is right."*

mcqs.question: In *Paradise Lost*, what bridge is constructed across Chaos immediately following the Fall of Adam and Eve?
options: A golden staircase built by the Archangel Gabriel
A broad highway linking Hell to Earth built by Sin and Death
A crystalline rainbow constructed by the Son of God
A wall of fire erected by the Cherubim
mcqs.explanation: In Book X, Sin and Death pave a broad, indestructible stone bridge over the dark abyss of Chaos, connecting Hell directly to the fallen earth to allow easy demonic passage.

mcqs.question: Which 18th-century literary club included Alexander Pope, Jonathan Swift, John Gay, Thomas Parnell, and Dr. John Arbuthnot?
mcqs.explanation: The Scriblerus Club was founded in 1714 by Pope, Swift, Gay, Arbuthnot, and Parnell to satirize pedantry and bad learning under the fictional persona of Martinus Scriblerus.

chapters.title: Unit II: Poetry — Chapter 14
chapters.subtitle: Pre-Romantic & Romantic Poetry

content.value: 1. Historical, Philosophical & Aesthetic Foundations

The Romantic movement in English literature (roughly spanning 1789 to 1832—from the outbreak of the French Revolution to the passage of the First Reform Bill) represented a cataclysmic rebellion against Augustan rationalism, neoclassical decorum, mechanistic empiricism, and the industrial desecration of nature.
1.1 The Revolutionary & Philosophical Crucible

- **The French Revolution (1789)**: The storming of the Bastille ignited utopian hopes among young English poets (Wordsworth famously wrote in *The Prelude*: *"Bliss was it in that dawn to be alive, / But to be young was very heaven!"*). The subsequent descent of the Revolution into the Reign of Terror (1793–94) and Napoleon's imperial tyranny forced English Romanticism into an introspective, psychological, and transcendental internalization of liberty.
- **The Industrial Revolution & Enclosure Acts**: The transformation of rural England into smoky manufacturing cities ("Dark Satanic Mills" in Blake) provoked an intense yearning for pastoral communion, untamed wild landscapes, and rustic simplicity.
- **Philosophical Underpinnings**:
  - **Jean-Jacques Rousseau**: The doctrine of natural human innocence corrupted by civilization (*"Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains"*), alongside the cult of sensibility (*The Confessions*).
  - **German Idealism (Kant, Schelling, Schlegel)**: Imported into England by Samuel Taylor Coleridge. The mind was no longer viewed as Locke's passive wax tablet (*tabula rasa*), but as an active, divine creator: **The Lamp** illuminating reality rather than **The Mirror** passively reflecting it (as M.H. Abrams famously formulated in *The Mirror and the Lamp*, 1953).

```
                      THE ROMANTIC AESTHETIC EVOLUTION
                                      │
    ┌─────────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┐
    ▼                                                                   ▼
THE TRANSITIONAL / PRE-ROMANTICS                         THE HIGH ROMANTIC FLOWERING
• The Graveyard School (Gray, Young, Blair)              • The First Generation (Lake Poets)
• Cult of Sensibility & Nature (Cowper, Thomson)           - William Wordsworth (Egoistical Sublime)
• Folk Ballads & Scottish Dialect (Robert Burns)           - S.T. Coleridge (Secondary Imagination)
• Radical Mythmaking & Illuminated Art (William Blake)     - Robert Southey
                                                         • The Second Generation (Radicals & Exiles)
                                                           - Lord Byron (Byronic Hero, Satire)
                                                           - P.B. Shelley (Radical Idealism, Platonism)
                                                           - John Keats (Negative Capability, Sensuousness)
```
1.2 The Two Generations of Romantics

1. **The First Generation (The Lake Poets: Wordsworth, Coleridge, Southey)**: Born in the 1770s; experienced the initial intoxicating hope and subsequent disillusionment of the French Revolution; settled into the rustic landscape of the Lake District; gradually evolved into political conservatism in later life.
2. **The Second Generation (Byron, Shelley, Keats)**: Born in the late 1780s and 1790s during the Napoleonic Wars; rebellious, anti-establishment, alienated from British conservative society; all died tragically young in Mediterranean exile (Keats in Rome at 25, Shelley in the Gulf of Spezia at 29, Byron in Missolonghi at 36).
2. The Pre-Romantics & The Graveyard School

Before the 1798 publication of *Lyrical Ballads*, a transitional generation of mid-eighteenth-century poets rebelled against the urban satire and closed heroic couplet of Pope, cultivating solitude, melancholy, nocturnal graveyards, and the sublime:
2.1 The Graveyard School

- **Edward Young (1683–1765)**: *Night-Thoughts on Life, Death, and Immortality* (1742–45; nine parts in blank verse). A sweeping, gloomy meditation on human mortality and Christian redemption composed in nocturnal solitude.
- **Robert Blair (1699–1746)**: *The Grave* (1743; 767 lines of blank verse), celebrating the macabre horrors of the tomb, illustrated famously by William Blake.
- **Thomas Gray (1716–1771)**: **"Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard"** (1751):
  - Composed in four-line iambic pentameter stanzas rhyming *abab* (**heroic quatrains** or **elegiac stanzas**).
  - Shifts poetic attention away from aristocratic monuments in Westminster Abbey to the unhonored, rustic graves of poor English villagers in Stoke Poges:
  - *"The Curfew tolls the knell of parting day, / The lowing herd wind slowly o'er the lea, / The plowman homeward plods his weary way, / And leaves the world to darkness and to me."*
  - Celebrates the unfulfilled potential of the poor:
  - *"Full many a gem of purest ray serene, / The dark unfathom'd caves of ocean bear: / Full many a flow'r is born to blush unseen, / And waste its sweetness on the desert air."*
  - Suggests that among the dead villagers might lie a mute inglorious Milton or an innocent Cromwell: *"Some mute inglorious Milton here may rest, / Some Cromwell guiltless of his country's blood."*
2.2 Robert Burns and William Cowper

- **William Cowper (1731–1800)**: *The Task* (1785; six books of blank verse). Celebrates domestic retreat, the English landscape, and evangelical piety: *"God made the country, and man made the town."* Wrote the tragic, harrowing spiritual elegy **"The Castaway"** (1799), identifying himself with a drowning sailor abandoned by God.
- **Robert Burns (1759–1796)**: The national poet of Scotland ("The Ploughman Poet"). Wrote in Scots and Scottish dialect, reviving traditional oral balladry and musical lyricism:
  - *Poems, Chiefly in the Scottish Dialect* (The Kilmarnock Edition, 1786).
  - **"Tam o' Shanter"** (1791): A rollicking mock-heroic narrative poem in octosyllabic couplets. The drunken farmer Tam stumbles upon a witches' coven dancing in the ruined kirk of Alloway, narrowly escaping the witch Nannie aboard his mare Meg (who loses her tail).
  - Immortal lyrics: *"A Red, Red Rose"*, *"Auld Lang Syne"*, *"To a Mouse"* (*"The best-laid schemes o' mice an' men / Gang aft agley"*), *"To a Louse"*, and *"Scots Wha Hae"*.
3. Exhaustive Author & Text Analyses: The Big Six
3.1 William Blake (1757–1827): The Visionary Printmaker

Engraver, painter, and visionary mystic who invented the technique of **illuminated printing** (relief etching), integrating poetry and visual art on a single copper plate:
- **Songs of Innocence and of Experience: Shewing the Two Contrary States of the Human Soul (1794)**:
  - *Innocence (1789)*: Represents the uncorrupted state of childhood, pastoral harmony, and Christ as the Lamb.
  - *Experience (1794)*: Represents the fallen, cynical world of social exploitation, institutional cruelty (the Church, the State), and industrial repression.
  - **The Paired Poems**:
    - **"The Lamb"** (*Innocence*): *"Little Lamb, who made thee? / Dost thou know who made thee?"* Celebrates Christ as gentle, meek, and child-like.
    - **"The Tyger"** (*Experience*): *"Tyger! Tyger! burning bright / In the forests of the night, / What immortal hand or eye / Could frame thy fearful symmetry?"* Poses the profound theological question of cosmic theodicy: *"Did he who made the Lamb make thee?"*
    - **"The Chimney Sweeper"** (both states): In *Innocence*, the sweep Tom Dacre dreams of an Angel liberating sweeps to play in green fields; in *Experience*, the sweep stands weeping in snow while his parents pray in church, exposing pious hypocrisy: *"They clothed me in the clothes of death, / And taught me to sing the notes of woe."*
    - **"London"** (*Experience*): The speaker wanders through "charter'd streets" near the "charter'd Thames", hearing the "mind-forg'd manacles" in every cry. Anatomizes four institutions of social oppression: the chimney sweep's cry blackening the Church, the hapless soldier's sigh running in blood down palace walls, and the youthful harlot's curse blasting the newborn infant and the "Marriage hearse".
- **The Marriage of Heaven and Hell (1790)**: Prose satire and visionary manifesto mocking Swedenborg. Subverts orthodox Christian morality:
  - Energy is eternal delight; Reason is the bound or outward circumference of Energy.
  - *Proverbs of Hell*: *"The road of excess leads to the palace of wisdom"*; *"The tygers of wrath are wiser than the horses of instruction."*
- **The Prophetic Books**: Mythological epics (*The Book of Urizen*, *America*, *Europe*, *Vala, or The Four Zoas*, *Milton*, *Jerusalem*). Created his own mythology: **Urizen** (the cold, tyrannical god of Reason and moral law), **Los** (the prophet of Imagination and poetic forge), **Orc** (the fiery spirit of revolutionary rebellion), and **Enitharmon** (Spiritual Beauty).
- **"And did those feet in ancient time"** (from the preface to *Milton*): The famous hymn celebrating the rebuilding of **Jerusalem** in "England's green & pleasant Land", combating the "Dark Satanic Mills".
3.2 William Wordsworth (1770–1850): The High Priest of Nature
Appointed Poet Laureate in 1843. Pioneered the **"Egoistical Sublime"** (John Keats's phrase), centering epic poetry entirely on the subjective development of the poet's own mind.

#### (A) Lyrical Ballads (1798; Preface 1800, 1802)
Co-authored with S.T. Coleridge, published anonymously in September 1798, inaugurating the English Romantic movement. Contained 23 poems (19 by Wordsworth, 4 by Coleridge, opening with *The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere* and concluding with Wordsworth's *Tintern Abbey*).
- **The 1800/1802 Preface**: The revolutionary poetic manifesto of Romanticism:
  - **Definition of Poetry**: *"Poetry is the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings: it takes its origin from emotion recollected in tranquillity."*
  - **Definition of the Poet**: *"A man speaking to men: a man, it is true, endued with more lively sensibility, more enthusiasm and tenderness, who has a greater knowledge of human nature, and a more comprehensive soul..."*
  - **Poetic Diction**: Rejection of artificial 18th-century "poetic diction" and gaudy personifications in favor of the **"real language of men in a state of vivid sensation"**, choosing "humble and rustic life" because in that condition the essential passions of the human heart find a simpler, uninhibited expression.

#### (B) Major Masterpieces
- **"Lines Composed a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey" (1798)**: 159 lines of blank verse composed during a walking tour of the Wye Valley with his sister **Dorothy Wordsworth**:
  - Traces Wordsworth's three psychological stages of relating to Nature:
    1. *Boyhood*: Animal pleasures, coarse nature, rushing like a roe over the mountains.
    2. *Youth*: Nature as an intense, unreflecting visual appetite, passion, and aching love (*"The sounding cataract / Haunted me like a passion"*).
    3. *Maturity*: Nature spiritualized; hearing *"The still, sad music of humanity, / Nor harsh nor grating, though of ample power / To chasten and subdue"*, culminating in his sublime pantheistic creed:
       > *"And I have felt / A presence that disturbs me with the joy / Of elevated thoughts; a sense sublime / Of something far more deeply interfused, / Whose dwelling is the light of setting suns, / And the round ocean and the living air, / And the blue sky, and in the mind of man: / A motion and a spirit, that impels / All thinking things, all objects of all thought, / And rolls through all things."*
- **"Ode: Intimations of Immortality from Recollections of Early Childhood" (1807)**:
  - An eleven-stanza irregular Pindaric ode meditating on the loss of childhood's visionary gleam.
  - Adopts the Neoplatonic doctrine of **anamnesis** (pre-existence of the soul):
    > *"Our birth is but a sleep and a forgetting: / The Soul that rises with us, our life's Star, / Hath had elsewhere its setting, / And cometh from afar: / Not in entire forgetfulness, / And not in utter nakedness, / But trailing clouds of glory do we come / From God, who is our home: / Heaven lies about us in our infancy! / Shades of the prison-house begin to close / Upon the growing Boy."*
  - Concludes that philosophic maturity brings compensation through human empathy: *"Thanks to the human heart by which we live, / Thanks to its tenderness, its joys, and fears, / To me the meanest flower that blows can give / Thoughts that do often lie too deep for tears."*
- **The Prelude, or Growth of a Poet's Mind (composed 1798–1805; pub. posthumously 1850)**:
  - Conceived as an autobiographical preparatory poem to a colossal, never-completed philosophical epic titled *The Recluse*.
  - Versions: The 1799 Two-Part Prelude; the **1805 Thirteen-Book Prelude**; and the polished **18speculative 14-book 1850 text** (titled by his widow Mary Wordsworth).
  - Masterpiece of psychological epic in blank verse. Contains the famous **"Spots of Time"**—epiphanic childhood memories of profound emotional and moral power:
    - *The Stolen Boat Episode*: The young William rows out on Ullswater lake at night; a huge black peak rears its head, seeming to pursue him like a living creature, inducing days of solitary moral terror.
    - *The Ice-Skating Episode*; *The Crossing of the Alps (Simplon Pass)*; *The Vision on Mount Snowdon* (Book XIV, where the moonlit sea of mist becomes an emblem of the sovereign human imagination).
3.3 Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834): The Mystic of the Supernatural

Philosopher, literary critic, and poet who explored the uncanny, exotic, and supernatural realms of the human subconscious:
- **Critical Distinction: Fancy vs. Imagination (Biographia Literaria, 1817, Chapter XIII)**:
  - **Fancy**: A mere mechanical mode of memory, aggregating and recombining fixed, dead images without changing their nature (*associative*).
  - **Primary Imagination**: The universal living power of human perception, a repetition in the finite mind of the eternal act of creation in the infinite "I AM".
  - **Secondary Imagination**: The conscious, poetic agency that *"dissolves, diffuses, dissipates, in order to recreate; or where this process is rendered impossible, yet still at all events it struggles to idealize and to unify. It is essentially vital."*
  - **Willing Suspension of Disbelief**: Coleridge's famous phrase in Chapter XIV explaining his goal in *Lyrical Ballads* to treat supernatural subjects with human truth, procuring for shadows of imagination *"that willing suspension of disbelief for the moment, which constitutes poetic faith."*
- **The Mystery Poems**:
  - **"The Rime of the Ancient Mariner" (1798)**: Seven parts in traditional ballad meter (*abcb*).
    - An ancient mariner stops a Wedding Guest to recount his doomed voyage to the Antarctic. He irrationally shoots the sacred **Albatross** with his crossbow, bringing a supernatural curse upon the ship.
    - The ship is becalmed under a burning sun (*"Water, water, every where, / Nor any drop to drink"*). The skeleton ship approaches carrying **Death** and **Life-in-Death**, who dicing win the crew and the Mariner respectively. 200 sailors drop dead.
    - *The Turning Point*: In moonlight, the isolated Mariner watches the luminous water-snakes in the sea; struck by their beauty, he blesses them unaware. The Albatross falls from his neck into the sea; rain falls, and dead sailors are animated by angelic spirits.
    - *The Moral*: He is condemned to wander the world telling his tale: *"He prayeth best, who loveth best / All things both great and small; / For the dear God who loveth us, / He made and loveth all."*
  - **"Kubla Khan; or, A Vision in a Dream: A Fragment" (1797, pub. 1816)**:
    - Composed under the influence of an anodyne (opium) after reading Purchas's *Pilgrimage*. Interrupted during transcription by the infamous **"person on business from Porlock"**.
    - Depicts the Mongol emperor Kubla Khan decreeing a *"stately pleasure-dome"* in Xanadu where Alph, the sacred river, runs through caverns measureless to man down to a sunless sea. Counterpoints the artificial sunny dome with the subterranean caves of ice, and evokes the Abyssinian maid playing on her dulcimer on Mount Abora as the symbol of poetic inspiration.
  - **"Christabel" (1797–1800, pub. 1816)**: Unfinished gothic romance in accentual meter (four stresses per line regardless of syllable count). The pure maiden Christabel discovers the mysterious **Geraldine** in the woods at midnight, carrying her across the threshold of her father Sir Leoline's castle, where Geraldine's serpentine evil begins to hypnotically bewitch her.
- **The Conversation Poems**: Informal, blank-verse meditations tracing an emotional arc from domestic calm to cosmic meditation and back: *"The Eolian Harp"*, *"This Lime-Tree Bower My Prison"*, *"Frost at Midnight"*, and the grief-stricken elegy on the death of imagination, **"Dejection: An Ode"** (1802).
3.4 Lord Byron (George Gordon, 6th Baron Byron, 1788–1824): The Romantic Rebel
The most commercially successful, internationally famous, and politically flamboyant poet of the era.

#### (A) The Byronic Hero & Childe Harold's Pilgrimage (1812–1818)
- **Publication**: Published Cantos I & II in 1812: *"I awoke one morning and found myself famous."* Composed in the 9-line **Spenserian stanza** (*ababbcbcc*).
- **The Byronic Hero Archetype**: A brooding, aristocratic outcast, intellectually superior, cynical, mysterious, laden with an unnameable past guilt or dark secret, defiant of societal laws and religious orthodoxies, capable of deep passion but consumed by misanthropy and world-weariness (exemplified in Childe Harold, Manfred, Cain, and the Oriental tales: *The Giaour*, *The Corsair*, *Lara*).

#### (B) Don Juan (1819–1824; 16 Cantos + 17th unfinished)
Byron's epic masterpiece of satirical realism, written in **Ottava Rima** (*abababcc*):
- **The Comic Reversal**: Reverses the legendary Spanish libertine myth: instead of Juan being an active predatory seducer, Byron's Don Juan is an innocent, handsome youth repeatedly seduced by dominant women (Donna Julia in Seville, Haidée on the Greek island, Gulbeyaz in the Turkish harem, Catherine the Great in Saint Petersburg, Lady Adeline in England).
- **The Digressive Satire**: Celebrated for the conversational ease of its closing rhyming couplets, deploying biting irony against political tyranny, war, hypocrisy, and contemporary poets (especially the Lake Poets Southey, Wordsworth, and Coleridge):
  > *"Bob Southey! You're a poet—poet-laureate, / And representative of all the race; / Although 'tis true that you're turn'd out a Tory at / Last—yours has lately been a common case."*
3.5 Percy Bysshe Shelley (1792–1822): The Unacknowledged Legislator
Radical philosophical atheist, political utopian, and lyric genius of incandescent Platonic idealism. Expelled from Oxford in 1811 for co-authoring the pamphlet *The Necessity of Atheism*.

#### (A) Major Lyrics & Odes
- **"Ozymandias" (1818)**: A 14-line sonnet with an unconventional rhyme scheme (*ababacdcedefef*). A traveler from an antique land recounts seeing two trunkless legs of stone in the desert, and a shattered face bearing a wrinkled lip and sneer of cold command. The pedestal reads: *"My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings; / Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!"* Nothing beside remains; boundless and bare, the lone and level sands stretch far away—a sublime monument to the inevitable decay of tyrannical political power.
- **"Ode to the West Wind" (1819)**: Composed in five 14-line sections written in **Terza Rima** (*aba bcb cdc ded ee*):
  - Sections 1–3 address the West Wind as **"Destroyer and Preserver"**, sweeping autumn leaves across the earth, driving storm clouds across the sky, and waking the Mediterranean from summer dreams.
  - Section 4: The poet identifies his own wounded, bleeding spirit with the wind: *"I fall upon the thorns of life! I bleed!"*
  - Section 5: The poet begs the wind to make him its lyre, scattering his revolutionary thoughts like sparks from an unextinguished hearth across the universe, ending with the immortal prophecy of political and spiritual resurrection:
    > *"Scatter, as from an unextinguish'd hearth / Ashes and sparks, my words among mankind! / Be through my lips to unawaken'd earth / The trumpet of a prophecy! O Wind, / If Winter comes, can Spring be far behind?"*
- **"To a Skylark" (1820)**: 21 five-line stanzas (*ababb*) addressing the bird as an unbodied joy (*"Hail to thee, blithe Spirit! / Bird thou never wert"*). Contrasts human suffering with the bird's pure ecstasy: *"Our sincerest laughter / With some pain is fraught; / Our sweetest songs are those that tell of saddest thought."*

#### (B) Mythological Drama & Elegy
- **Prometheus Unbound (1820)**: Four-act lyrical drama in blank verse. Reverses Aeschylus's lost tragedy: Prometheus refuses to compromise with the tyrant Jupiter, renouncing his former curse through love and forgiveness. Jupiter is overthrown by Demogorgon (Primal Necessity), ushering in an era of universal cosmic love and liberation.
- **Adonais: An Elegy on the Death of John Keats (1821)**: Composed in 55 **Spenserian stanzas** (*ababbcbcc*). Modeled on the classical Greek pastoral elegies of Bion and Moschus.
  - Mourns Keats, blaming his death on brutal Tory reviews in the *Quarterly Review* and *Blackwood's Magazine*.
  - Transforms from grief into triumphant Platonic apotheosis: Keats is not dead; it is the living mortals who sleep in the nightmare of earthly life:
    > *"Peace, peace! he is not dead, he doth not sleep— / He hath awakened from the dream of life— / 'Tis we, who lost in stormy visions, keep / With phantoms an unprofitable strife... / The One remains, the many change and pass; / Heaven's light forever shines, Earth's shadows fly; / Life, like a dome of many-colour'd glass, / Stains the white radiance of Eternity, / Until Death tramples it to fragments."*
- **A Defence of Poetry (1821, pub. 1840)**: Written in response to his friend Thomas Love Peacock's satirical essay *"The Four Ages of Poetry"*. Shelley defends poetry as the divine faculty of imagination that awakens moral empathy, concluding with the famous aphorism:
  > *"Poets are the unacknowledged legislators of the world."*
3.6 John Keats (1795–1821): The Sensuous Alchemist of Art
Trained as an apothecary-surgeon at Guy's Hospital; died of tuberculosis in Rome at the age of 25. Requested his tombstone bear the epitaph: *"Here lies One Whose Name was writ in Water."*

#### (A) Core Critical Theories (From Letters)
- **Negative Capability**: Formulated in a December 1817 letter to his brothers George and Thomas:
  > *"Negative Capability, that is when man is capable of being in uncertainties, Mysteries, doubts, without any irritable reaching after fact & reason."* Keats cited William Shakespeare as the supreme exemplar, contrasting him with Coleridge's need for philosophical certainty.
- **The Chameleon Poet**: In an 1818 letter to Richard Woodhouse, Keats defined the poetic character: *"It has no self—it is every thing and nothing—It has no character... It enjoys light and shade; it lives in gusto, be it foul or fair, high or low, rich or poor, mean or elevated. It has as much delight in conceiving an Iago as an Imogen."* Contrasted with Wordsworth's "Egoistical Sublime".
- **The Vale of Soul-Making**: In an 1819 letter, Keats rejected the idea of the world as a "vale of tears", redefining it as a "Vale of Soul-making", where painful mortal experience tempers the human spark into an authentic soul.

#### (B) The Great Odes of 1819 (The Annus Mirabilis)
Composed between April and September 1819:
1. **"Ode to a Nightingale"** (May 1819; 8 ten-line stanzas):
   - Opens in a state of drowsy numbness: *"My heart aches, and a drowsy numbness pains / My sense, as though of hemlock I had drunk"*.
   - Explores escape through wine (*a draught of vintage*), but rejects Bacchus in favor of the *"viewless wings of Poesy"*.
   - In the dark forest, the poet cannot see the flowers, but smells them through synaesthetic sensation (*"I cannot see what flowers are at my feet"*).
   - Meditates on death: *"for many a time / I have been half in love with easeful Death"*.
   - Celebrates the bird's immortality: *"Thou wast not born for death, immortal Bird! / No hungry generations tread thee down"*; heard by ancient emperor and the biblical Ruth weeping in the alien corn.
   - The word **"Forlorn!"** acts like a tolling bell snapping him back to reality: *"Was it a vision, or a waking dream? / Fled is that music:—Do I wake or sleep?"*
2. **"Ode on a Grecian Urn"** (May 1819; 5 ten-line stanzas):
   - Addresses the ancient marble urn as a *"still unravish'd bride of quietness, / Thou foster-child of silence and slow time"*.
   - Meditates on the paradox of art vs. life: the figures carved on the urn are frozen in eternal anticipation: the Bold Lover can never kiss the maiden, but her beauty will never fade (*"She cannot fade, though thou hast not thy bliss, / For ever wilt thou love, and she be fair!"*).
   - In Stanza IV, visits the deserted, silent town left empty by the sacrificial procession.
   - Concludes with the famous aesthetic crux:
     > *"Beauty is truth, truth beauty,—that is all / Ye know on earth, and all ye need to know."*
3. **"Ode on Melancholy"** (May 1819):
   - Instructs the reader not to go to Lethe or poison oneself with nightshade to escape sorrow.
   - True Melancholy dwells with Beauty—beauty that must die—and Joy whose hand is ever at his lips bidding adieu. Only he who can burst Joy's grape against his palate can taste Melancholy's sovereign power.
4. **"Ode to Psyche"**: Keats builds a mental sanctuary in his mind for Psyche, the neglected goddess of the soul.
5. **"To Autumn"** (September 1819; 3 eleven-line stanzas):
   - The most serenely objective and structurally perfect of Keats's odes.
   - Contains zero personal complaints or melancholy longings for escape.
   - Stanza 1: Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness (tactile ripeness, cottage trees bending with apples, bees).
   - Stanza 2: Autumn personified as a rustic worker (sitting careless on a granary floor, asleep on a half-reaped furrow, watching the cider-press).
   - Stanza 3: Sunset and music: *"Where are the songs of Spring? Ay, where are they? / Think not of them, thou hast thy music too"*; small gnats mourning in a wailful choir, full-grown lambs bleating, and gathering swallows twittering in the skies.
4. Technical Conventions, Poetic Forms & Prosody
4.1 Major Romantic Verse Forms

- **The Greater Romantic Lyric**: Formulated by M.H. Abrams. A tripartite meditative lyric structure (exemplified in *Tintern Abbey*, *Frost at Midnight*, *Ode to the West Wind*):
  1. *Outset*: Description of a particular, localized natural scene.
  2. *Turn*: An inward journey of memory, meditation, or emotional crisis.
  3. *Return*: Return to the original scene, but transformed by spiritual wisdom and renewed imaginative resolution.
- **Terza Rima**: A three-line interlocking stanza rhyming *aba bcb cdc ded ee*, imported from Dante's *Divine Comedy*, perfected in English by Shelley in *Ode to the West Wind* and *The Triumph of Life*.
- **Ottava Rima**: An eight-line stanza rhyming *abababcc*, imported from Italian epic romance (Ariosto, Pulci), weaponized by Lord Byron for comic digressions and epigrammatic couplet punchlines in *Don Juan*.
- **The Romantic Ode**:
  - *Pindaric Ode*: Irregular strophes, antistrophes, and epodes (*Wordsworth's Immortality Ode*).
  - *Horatian Ode*: Symmetrical, uniform stanzas (*Keats's Odes*).
4.2 Key Romantic Concepts & Rhetorical Tropes

- **Synaesthesia**: The blending or crossing of sensory modalities in language (e.g., Keats's *"taste the country green"*, *"soft-dying day"*, *"fragrant darkness"*).
- **The Sublime**: Formulated by Edmund Burke (*A Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful*, 1757) and Immanuel Kant. Contrasted with the "Beautiful" (which is small, smooth, orderly, and pleasing), the "Sublime" is vast, dark, infinite, terrifying, and overwhelming, evoking awe and insignificance before nature's power.
- **Negative Capability**: Keats's aesthetic principle of remaining content in uncertainties without irritatingly grasping after rational explanations.
5. Comparative Analysis Matrices
5.1 First Generation vs. Second Generation Romantics

| Dimension | First Generation (Wordsworth, Coleridge, Southey) | Second Generation (Byron, Shelley, Keats) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Historical Experience** | Hope in 1789 French Revolution followed by disillusionment | Reared under the reactionary Napoleonic Wars and Tory repression |
| **Political Arc** | Radical young republicans turning into conservative patriots | Lifelong political radicals, exiles, and social iconoclasts |
| **Landscape / Setting** | Rural England, Lake District, Quantock Hills, Wales | Mediterranean, Italy, Switzerland, Greece, classical ruins |
| **Aesthetic Center** | Domestic nature, rustic speech, psychological introspection | Satire, heroic defiance, mythic liberation, pure aesthetic beauty |
| **Fate / Lifespan** | Lived to advanced old age (Wordsworth died at 80) | Died tragically young in foreign exile (Keats 25, Shelley 29, Byron 36) |
5.2 The Aesthetic Matrix of the Second Generation

| Feature | Lord Byron | Percy Bysshe Shelley | John Keats |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Dominant Form** | Ottava Rima Satire & Spenserian Travelogue | Terza Rima, Blank Verse Drama, Lyric Odes | The Ten-Line Horatian Ode, Narrative Romances |
| **Heroic Archetype** | The Byronic Hero (Manfred, Childe Harold) | The Unbound Titan / Liberator (Prometheus) | The Absorbed Observer / Sensitive Soul (Endymion) |
| **Philosophical Base** | Augustan Skepticism (Pope), Realism, Misanthropy | Radical Platonism, Godwinian Necessitarianism | Sensuous Aestheticism, Negative Capability |
| **Treatment of Nature** | A mirror for turbulent human passions | A cosmic dynamo of invisible, revolutionary energy | A rich sensory tapestry of tactile, auditory, and visual beauty |
| **View of the Poet** | The aristocratic, ironical, worldly commentator | The unacknowledged legislator of the universe | The chameleon poet with no rigid personal identity |

7. 50 High-Yield Exam One-Liners & Trap Alerts

1. **Lyrical Ballads Date**: Published in September **1798**; contained 23 poems (19 by Wordsworth, 4 by Coleridge).
2. **First and Last Poems in 1798**: Opened with Coleridge's *The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere* and concluded with Wordsworth's *Tintern Abbey*.
3. **Wordsworth's Emotion Axiom**: *"Poetry is the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings: it takes its origin from emotion recollected in tranquillity"* appears in the 1800/1802 Preface.
4. **M.H. Abrams's Landmark Book**: *The Mirror and the Lamp* (1953) contrasts the Neoclassical mind as a mirror reflecting external nature with the Romantic mind as a lamp illuminating it.
5. **The Egoistical Sublime**: Keats coined the term "Egoistical Sublime" in an 1818 letter to describe William Wordsworth's intense self-centering.
6. **Dorothy Wordsworth's Journals**: Dorothy's *Grasmere Journals* provided the raw observational notes for many of William's poems, including "I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud" (*Daffodils*).
7. **The Wye River**: *Tintern Abbey* is subtitled: *Lines Composed a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey, on Revisiting the Banks of the Wye during a Tour. July 13, 1798*.
8. **Three Stages in Tintern Abbey**: Boyhood (animal pleasures), Youth (dizzy raptures/visual aching love), Maturity (the still, sad music of humanity / deeply interfused spirit).
9. **Spots of Time**: In *The Prelude* (Book XII), Wordsworth defines "spots of time" as profound childhood memories that nourish and restore the mind throughout life.
10. **The Subtitle of The Prelude**: Subtitled *Growth of a Poet's Mind*; addressed throughout to Samuel Taylor Coleridge.
11. **The Prelude's Original Naming**: Wordsworth always referred to it in life as "the poem on my own life" or "the poem to Coleridge"; his widow Mary Wordsworth named it *The Prelude* upon publication in 1850.
12. **The Simplon Pass**: In Book VI of *The Prelude*, Wordsworth crosses the Alps via the Simplon Pass without realizing it, giving rise to a sublime hymn to the Imagination.
13. **Primary vs. Secondary Imagination**: Coleridge defined Primary Imagination as the living power of all human perception, and Secondary Imagination as the conscious poetic power that "dissolves, diffuses, dissipates, in order to recreate" (*Biographia Literaria*, Ch. XIII).
14. **Willing Suspension of Disbelief**: Coleridge formulated this phrase in *Biographia Literaria* (Ch. XIV) to describe the poetic faith granted to supernatural tales.
15. **The Albatross's Slaying**: In *The Rime of the Ancient Mariner*, the Mariner kills the bird with a **crossbow** for no rational reason.
16. **The Dice Game in Ancient Mariner**: **Life-in-Death** (a pale woman with golden hair and red lips) wins the Mariner, while **Death** wins the 200 crew members.
17. **The Mariner's Redemption Turn**: Occurs when he observes the slimy **water-snakes** in the moonlit ocean and blesses them unaware in his heart, allowing the Albatross to drop into the sea.
18. **The Person from Porlock**: The unnamed visitor who interrupted Coleridge while writing down *Kubla Khan*, causing the loss of the rest of his opium-induced vision.
19. **Kubla Khan's Sacred River**: The sacred river in Xanadu is named **Alph**, which runs through caverns measureless to man down to a sunless sea.
